**Given:** The coefficient-complete carrier, endomorphism filtration, coderivations, and square-zero degree-one $D$ in the stated definition.

1.1 For a uniformly Cauchy sequence $T_m$ in $E$, each $T_m(c)$ is Cauchy in $C_B$, because $T_m-T_j\in F^pE$ eventually for every $p$. Define $T(c)=\lim_m T_m(c)$. Limits preserve addition, $B$-linearity, and each closed $F^qC_B$. Thus $T$ preserves the filtration and is continuous. If $T_m-T_j\in F^pE$ for all sufficiently large $j$, passing to the limit on every $F^qC_B$ gives $T_m-T\in F^pE$. This proves completeness; if $T\in\bigcap_pF^pE$, every $T(c)$ belongs to $\bigcap_pF^pC_B=0$, proving separation. [given, construct]

2.1 If $P\in F^pE$ and $Q\in F^qE$, then $PQ(F^rC_B)\subseteq P(F^{q+r}C_B)\subseteq F^{p+q+r}C_B$, proving multiplicativity. The coderivation equation, the counit equation, and evaluation at $1_C$ are closed conditions: reduce each equation modulo $F^n$ in its explicitly completed target, where sufficiently close maps agree. Consequently $\mathfrak l$ and every $F^p\mathfrak l$ are closed and complete in their induced filtration. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $p=|P|$, $q=|Q|$. For coderivations, the graded tensor composition rule gives $\Delta PQ=(PQ\otimes1+P\otimes Q+(-1)^{pq}Q\otimes P+1\otimes PQ)\Delta$. Subtracting $(-1)^{pq}\Delta QP$ cancels the two mixed terms and gives $\Delta[P,Q]=([P,Q]\otimes1+1\otimes[P,Q])\Delta$. Also $[P,Q](1_C)=0$ and $\epsilon[P,Q]=0$. Thus coderivations are closed under the commutator, and multiplicativity proves the additive filtration bound. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The commutator is graded skew because $[P,Q]=-(-1)^{pq}[Q,P]$. For $|R|=r$, direct expansion of $[P,[Q,R]]$ is $PQR-(-1)^{qr}PRQ-(-1)^{p(q+r)}QRP+(-1)^{p(q+r)+qr}RQP$. The expansion of $\bigl[ [P,Q],R\bigr]$ is $PQR-(-1)^{pq}QPR-(-1)^{(p+q)r}RPQ+(-1)^{(p+q)r+pq}RQP$. The expansion of $(-1)^{pq}[Q,[P,R]]$ is $(-1)^{pq}QPR-(-1)^{pq+pr}QRP-(-1)^{qr}PRQ+(-1)^{qr+pr}RPQ$. The $QPR$ and $RPQ$ terms cancel in the last two expressions; the other four agree with the first expression. This proves the graded Jacobi identity in derivation form, with all signs explicit. [step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For homogeneous $T$ of degree $t$, expanding $[D,[D,T]]$ gives $D^2T-TD^2$, since the two $DTD$ terms have coefficients $-(-1)^t$ and $+(-1)^t$. Hence $d^2T=0$. Substituting $P=D$ into the Jacobi identity proved in step 4.1 gives $d[P,Q]=[dP,Q]+(-1)^{|P|}[P,dQ]$. Because $D$ preserves each coefficient filtration, composition with $D$ and hence $d$ preserve every $F^pE$ and every $F^p\mathfrak l$. [given, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The preceding steps prove all graded Lie, differential, completeness, and filtration axioms on $F^1\mathfrak l$. In each quotient by $F^n$, any bracket with at least $n$ positive-order entries vanishes by the additive bound. Thus the positive filtration is pronilpotent as well as complete, as claimed. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1] ∎

**Given:** A complete multiplicatively filtered unital associative algebra $E$, $X,N\in F^1E$, and $T\in E$.

1.1 The terms $X^j$ and $N^j$ belong to $F^jE$. Therefore all displayed series have finite reductions modulo every $F^nE$ and define unique limits. Multiplication respects these limits because the filtration is multiplicative. In particular any one-variable formal series with rational coefficients and zero-order constant defined in $k$ can be evaluated at a positive-order element: each coefficient calculation becomes finite in every quotient. [given, construct]

1.2 In $\mathbb Q[\![t]\!]$, define $\ell(t)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j-1}t^j/j$. Termwise differentiation gives $\ell'(t)=(1+t)^{-1}$. The formal chain rule, obtained by expanding products coefficient by coefficient, gives $h'=h/(1+t)$ for $h=\exp\ell(t)$ and $h(0)=1$. From $(1+t)h'=h$ the coefficient recursion gives $h=1+t$: its coefficient of $t$ is $1$ and every higher coefficient is zero. Also the formal derivative of $\ell(\exp(t)-1)$ is $1$ and its constant coefficient is zero, so $\ell(\exp(t)-1)=t$. Each assertion is an identity of scalar coefficient series. [algebra]

1.3 Induction on $r$ proves $(\operatorname{ad}_X)^r(T)=\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j\binom rjX^{r-j}TX^j$: the induction step multiplies once on the left and subtracts once on the right, and Pascal's identity collects the overlapping terms. Every summand has filtration order at least $r$, even if $T$ has order zero, so the resulting exponential series converges. [given, algebra]

2.1 Substitute $N$ and $X$ into the two scalar identities modulo $F^nE$ and pass to the inverse limit, using step 1.1. This proves $\exp(\log(1+N))=1+N$ and $\log(\exp X)=X$. The substitution is sound in the noncommutative algebra because every identity involves powers of one fixed element only. The coefficient of total degree $r>0$ in $\exp(X)\exp(-X)$ is $X^r\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j/(j!(r-j)!)=0$; the degree-zero coefficient is $1$. Thus the exponential inverse is $\exp(-X)$ and both inverse bijections have the stated domains. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Expanding $\exp(X)T\exp(-X)$ modulo $F^nE$ and collecting the terms containing a total of $r$ copies of $X$ gives $\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^jX^{r-j}TX^j/((r-j)!j!)=(\operatorname{ad}_X)^r(T)/r!$. Passing to limits gives the conjugation identity. If $E$ is graded and $|X|=0$, its graded commutator with $T$ is exactly the ordinary commutator used here, so the same proof applies in every homogeneous degree. [step 1.1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The carrier and allowed automorphisms in the stated definition.

1.1 The complete filtered endomorphism algebra and its closed coderivation subspace are supplied by [[lem-complete-coderivations-form-a-filtered-differential-graded-lie-algebra]]. Thus [[lem-noncommutative-filtered-exponential-and-logarithm]] defines inverse exponential and logarithm series on positive-order degree-zero endomorphisms. All subsequent identities can be checked in $C_n=C\otimes_k B/I^n$ and its tensor target and then passed to limits. [given, construct]

1.2 Conversely, let $G$ be allowed and $N=G-\operatorname{id}$. On $C_n$, $N^n=0$. Define the endomorphism-valued polynomial $P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom tjN^j$. For every nonnegative integer $m$, the finite binomial theorem gives $P_n(m)=G^m$. Since $G^m$ is a counital coaugmented coalgebra map, $\Delta P_n(m)=(P_n(m)\otimes P_n(m))\Delta$, $P_n(m)(1_C)=1_C$, and $\epsilon P_n(m)=\epsilon$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For $X\in F^1\mathfrak l^0$, induction on $j$ using its coderivation equation gives $\Delta X^j=(X\otimes1+1\otimes X)^j\Delta$. The operators $X\otimes1$ and $1\otimes X$ commute because $X$ has degree zero. Each is of positive coefficient order, so the exponential and binomial calculations are finite in each quotient. Consequently $\Delta\exp X=(\exp X\otimes\exp X)\Delta$. Also $\exp X(1_C)=1_C$ and $\epsilon\exp X=\epsilon$, because every positive power of $X$ kills $1_C$ and is killed by $\epsilon$. Its inverse $\exp(-X)$ has the same properties. Hence exponential gives an allowed automorphism. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Each difference in these three identities is a polynomial in $t$ with coefficients in a $k$-vector space of maps. A polynomial of degree at most $a$ with such coefficients vanishing at $a+1$ distinct nonnegative integers has zero coefficients: apply the inverse of their scalar Vandermonde matrix over the characteristic-zero field $k$. This does not require finite-dimensional map spaces or any domain property of $B/I^n$. Therefore the identities of step 1.2 hold as polynomial identities for the indeterminate $t$. [step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Differentiate those polynomial identities at $t=0$. Since $P_n(0)=\operatorname{id}$, the result is $\Delta P_n'(0)=(P_n'(0)\otimes1+1\otimes P_n'(0))\Delta$, $P_n'(0)(1_C)=0$, and $\epsilon P_n'(0)=0$. For $j\ge1$, differentiation of $t(t-1)\cdots(t-j+1)/j!$ at zero gives $(-1)^{j-1}/j$. Thus $P_n'(0)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(-1)^{j-1}N^j/j$, exactly the reduction of $\log G$. [step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 These reductions are compatible for all $n$, and the coderivation, counit, and coaugmentation identities are closed in the completed targets. Therefore $\log G\in F^1\mathfrak l^0$. Step 1.1 gives inverse identities for the underlying endomorphisms, and step 2.1 shows that every positive-order degree-zero coderivation exponentiates into the allowed group. The restrictions are therefore mutually inverse bijections onto the entire stated group. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

**Given:** The stated coefficient-complete deformation data and $\mathfrak g=F^1\mathfrak l$.

1.1 By [[lem-complete-coderivations-form-a-filtered-differential-graded-lie-algebra]], $\mathfrak g$ is a complete filtered differential graded Lie algebra. Since $D$ and $R$ have degree one and $D^2=0$, direct expansion gives $(D+R)^2=DR+RD+R^2=dR+[R,R]/2$. Thus the displayed assignment is an object bijection, with inverse subtraction of $D$. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [[thm-coalgebra-automorphism-logarithms-are-coderivations]], every allowed $G$ has the unique form $G=\exp X$ with $X\in\mathfrak g^0$. The conjugation identity in [[lem-noncommutative-filtered-exponential-and-logarithm]] gives $G(D+R)G^{-1}=e^{\operatorname{ad}_X}(D+R)$. Since $[X,D]=-dX$, subtracting $D$ gives precisely the displayed action. Each term has increasing coefficient order. Conjugation preserves coderivations, their square-zero condition, and reduction to $D$, so this is an action on the object set. The group law is composition, transported through exp and log; no unproved BCH construction is needed. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $s:\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g[1]$ have degree $-1$. The shift lemma in the statement has $q_1(sx)=-s(dx)$ and $q_2(sx,sy)=(-1)^{|x|}s[x,y]$, with no higher operations. Hence the shifted curvature at $sR$ is $-s(dR+[R,R]/2)$, and its gauge vector with parameter $s\xi$ is $s(-d\xi+[\xi,R])$. Therefore the exact path equation of [[def-filtered-maurer-cartan-gauge-path]] is $R'=-d\xi+[\xi,R]$ for compatible polynomial coefficients $R(t)$ and $\xi(t)$, with $\xi(t)\in\mathfrak g^0[t]^{\wedge}=\varprojlim_n(\mathfrak g^0/F^n\mathfrak g^0)\otimes k[t]$. The scalar variable has degree zero, and algebraic integration divides $t^j$ by $j+1$ in the usual way. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Fix any such variable parameter $\xi(t)$ and write $E[t]^{\wedge}=\varprojlim_n(E/F^nE)\otimes k[t]$. Starting at $U_0=V_0=\operatorname{id}$, iterate $U_{a+1}(t)=\operatorname{id}+\int_0^t\xi(u)U_a(u)\,du$ and $V_{a+1}(t)=\operatorname{id}-\int_0^tV_a(u)\xi(u)\,du$. Multiplication by $\xi$ raises coefficient order by one, so successive differences have order at least $a+1$. Every quotient consequently stabilizes after finitely many iterations as a polynomial. Completeness gives unique solutions $U'=\xi U$, $V'=-V\xi$, $U(0)=V(0)=\operatorname{id}$. Uniqueness follows from the same integral equation: a difference in $F^a$ must lie in $F^{a+1}$, and the filtration is separated. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Differentiating gives $(VU)'=-V\xi U+V\xi U=0$, and its initial value is the identity, so $VU=\operatorname{id}$. Similarly $Z=UV-\operatorname{id}$ satisfies $Z'=\xi Z-Z\xi$ and $Z(0)=0$. Its integral equation raises coefficient order and forces $Z$ into every $F^a$, so $UV=\operatorname{id}$. Thus $V=U^{-1}$ as completed polynomial endomorphisms. [step 2.3, algebra]

4.1 In the completed tensor target put $H=\Delta U-(U\otimes U)\Delta$. The coderivation equation for $\xi$ and the product rule give $H'=(\xi\otimes1+1\otimes\xi)H$ and $H(0)=0$. Its integral equation forces successive coefficient orders and hence $H=0$. The same argument applied to $U(1_C)-1_C$ gives zero, using $\xi(1_C)=0$; and $(\epsilon U)'=\epsilon\xi U=0$ gives $\epsilon U=\epsilon$. Together with step 3.1 these prove that $U(t)$, and in particular $U(1)$, is an actual continuous coaugmented counital coalgebra automorphism congruent to the identity modulo $I$. All equations are quotientwise polynomial equations, not analytic-time claims. [step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For an initial deformation $K_0=D+R_0$, set $K(t)=U(t)K_0V(t)$. Differentiation gives $K'=[\xi,K]$, and $K(0)=K_0$. Consequently $R(t)=K(t)-D$ satisfies $R'=-d\xi+[\xi,R]$, and $K(t)^2=U K_0^2V=0$. Any other completed polynomial solution with the same parameter and initial value differs by $Z'= [\xi,Z]$, $Z(0)=0$, whose integral equation raises order and forces $Z=0$. Every elementary shifted gauge path is therefore this actual conjugation path for its own parameter and initial value. Its endpoints are conjugate by the allowed automorphism $U(1)$, and any finite chain of such paths remains conjugate by composition. [step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Conversely suppose an allowed $G$ carries $D+R_0$ to $D+R_1$. Step 2.1 gives $X=\log G\in\mathfrak g^0$. Set $U(t)=\exp(tX)$; its series is polynomial modulo each coefficient order, and step 2.1's coalgebra exponential theorem applies coefficientwise in $t$. The path $U(t)(D+R_0)U(t)^{-1}-D$ has parameter $\xi(t)=X$, is Maurer–Cartan for every $t$, and joins $R_0$ to $R_1$. Step 2.2 identifies it as an elementary shifted gauge path. Thus every allowed equivalence lies in the gauge relation. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Step 5.1 proves gauge-equivalent elements give equivalent deformations, and step 6.1 proves the converse. Combining this equivalence of relations with the object bijection in step 1.1 proves the claimed bijection on quotient classes, with the full equivalence group and displayed action of step 2.1. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 6.1] ∎

**Given:** The unital associative algebra, coefficient-complete carrier, and specified unit in the statement.

1.1 A homogeneous positive-arity Taylor map $f:(A[1])^{\otimes r}\to A[1]$ of degree $u$ extends by inserting $f$ in every consecutive block of a word, with sign $(-1)^{u(|v_1|+\cdots+|v_{i-1}|)}$ for a block starting at $i$. Each word has only finitely many such blocks. Splitting the output word shows the coderivation equation: the replaced block lies entirely on one side of a coproduct split, and its insertion sign agrees with that side's graded tensor action. Thus these formulas define the coderivation and extend continuously through coefficient completion. Conversely, applying the iterated reduced coproduct and projecting every factor to length one expresses the length-$j$ component of a coderivation as the sum with its length-one projection on one of the $j$ input factors. Its other components are the untouched factors. This follows by iterating the coderivation equation. It determines every length component uniquely, and proves there is no output of length greater than the input length because all $j$ factors must be nonempty. The argument holds at each coefficient quotient and then in the limit. Thus these Taylor maps give every coaugmented counital coderivation uniquely. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For clarity first allow graded $A$ and a degree-zero product. With $|sa|=|a|-1$, the binary map $b_\mu(sa,sb)=(-1)^{|a|}s\mu(a,b)$ has degree one and equals $-s\mu(s^{-1}\otimes s^{-1})$, since the tensor-map sign on $(sa,sb)$ is $(-1)^{|a|-1}$. Its insertion extension from step 1.1 is therefore precisely fixed, including signs. Its square is a coderivation because $b_\mu^2=[b_\mu,b_\mu]/2$ and coderivations are closed under graded commutators by [[lem-complete-coderivations-form-a-filtered-differential-graded-lie-algebra]]. Its only possibly nonzero Taylor projection has arity three and is $(-1)^{|b|}s(\mu(\mu(a,b),c)-\mu(a,\mu(b,c)))$. Indeed the first association has sign $(-1)^{|a|+|a|+|b|}$, and the second has sign $(-1)^{|a|-1+|b|+|a|}$. Thus its square is zero exactly when the product is associative. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Return to degree-zero $A$, so $A[1]$ has degree $-1$ and the displayed binary sign is $+1$. A Taylor map of degree $u$ from arity $r$ to length one can be nonzero only when $-r+u=-1$, namely $u=r-1$. Thus every degree-one coderivation is binary and every degree-zero coderivation is unary. Step 2.1 proves that $D=b_\mu$ is square-zero, and the same computation proves that a degree-one $R=b_\alpha$ satisfies $(D+R)^2=0$ exactly when $\mu+\alpha$ is associative. A continuous bilinear map is understood on $M\widehat\otimes_B M=\varprojlim_n(A^{\otimes2}\otimes_k B/I^n)$; the condition $R\in F^1$ says its coefficient image lies in $F^1M$. No naive algebraic tensor of a Hom space with $I$ is used. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For an ordinary $r$-cochain $f$, denote the Taylor coderivation with projection $q_f(sa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes sa_r)=sf(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ by $q_f$; it has degree $r-1$. Call $f$ normalized when any argument $e$ makes it zero. A Taylor insertion contributing to $q_fq_g$ has the form $f(a_1,\ldots,g(a_i,\ldots,a_{i+t-1}),\ldots,a_{r+t-1})$, up to its specified sign. If a unit argument lies inside the inserted block, $g$ vanishes; if outside, a remaining argument of $f$ is the unit and $f$ vanishes. Thus every insertion of normalized cochains is normalized separately, and so are their commutators. Evaluation with any input fixed to $e$ is a closed continuous condition. Hence $\mathfrak n$ is a closed graded Lie subalgebra with the inherited additive filtration bound. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 A degree-zero coalgebra map $G$ on this carrier is determined by its length-one projection, and that projection can be nonzero only on arity one, since all inputs of arity $r$ have degree $-r$ and $B$ has degree zero. To justify the determination explicitly, apply the iterated coproduct of $G$ and project its $j$ outputs to length one; the resulting length-$j$ component is the $j$-fold tensor of the length-one projection applied to the iterated coproduct of the input. Coaugmentation and counit fix the length-zero part. Hence $G=T^c(g)$ for the unary map $g:M\to M$; it is an allowed automorphism exactly when $g$ is continuous, invertible, and congruent to the identity modulo $I$. Conversely that tensor extension is a coalgebra automorphism by deconcatenation, with inverse $T^c(g^{-1})$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Although $b_\mu$ is not normalized, its commutator preserves normalization. Write the usual Hochschild differential as $(\delta_\mu f)(a_1,\ldots,a_{r+1})=a_1f(a_2,\ldots,a_{r+1})+\sum_{i=1}^r(-1)^if(a_1,\ldots,a_ia_{i+1},\ldots,a_{r+1})+(-1)^{r+1}f(a_1,\ldots,a_r)a_{r+1}$. The insertion convention gives exactly $\pi_1[b_\mu,q_f](sa_1,\ldots,sa_{r+1})=(-1)^{r-1}s(\delta_\mu f)(a_1,\ldots,a_{r+1})$. Indeed the left outer product has coefficient $(-1)^{r-1}$, from moving $q_f$ past $sa_1$; the right outer product has coefficient $+1$; and the $i$-th adjacent multiplication term in $-(-1)^{r-1}q_fb_\mu$ has coefficient $(-1)^{r+i-1}$. These are exactly the asserted common sign times the Hochschild coefficients. [step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra]

5.2 A degree-zero $X\in F^1\mathfrak n$ is $q_\xi$ for a continuous unary $\xi$ with $\xi(e)=0$. Since $\xi^j(e)=0$ for all $j\ge1$, $g=\exp\xi$ fixes $e$. Conversely if $g\equiv\operatorname{id}\pmod I$ fixes $e$, then $(g-\operatorname{id})(e)=0$ and every positive power does too, so $\log(g)(e)=0$. Both series converge by [[lem-noncommutative-filtered-exponential-and-logarithm]], applied to the unary complete endomorphism algebra or to length one in $C_B$. Also $\exp(q_\xi)=T^c(\exp\xi)$: the left side is a coalgebra map by [[thm-coalgebra-automorphism-logarithms-are-coderivations]], has unary projection $\exp\xi$, and is determined by that projection by step 4.2. Applying the inverse logarithm proves $\log(T^c(g))=q_{\log(g)}$. Consequently exponentials of $F^1\mathfrak n^0$ give exactly all the required unit-preserving changes of variables, including the reverse implication that $\exp\xi(e)=e$ forces $\xi(e)=0$. [step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 If the unit occurs at an interior position $2\le j\le r$, the adjacent multiplication terms $i=j-1$ and $i=j$ in $\delta_\mu f$ have identical remaining arguments and opposite signs; every other term retains the unit inside $f$ and vanishes. If $j=1$, the first outer product term cancels the $i=1$ multiplication term, using $ef=f$. If $j=r+1$, the $i=r$ multiplication term cancels the last outer product term, using $fe=f$. In both endpoint cases all remaining terms vanish by normalization. These arguments also include $r=1$, where only the endpoint cases occur. Thus $\delta_\mu$ preserves normalization and $[D,\mathfrak n]\subseteq\mathfrak n$. Closedness in step 4.1 and [[lem-complete-coderivations-form-a-filtered-differential-graded-lie-algebra]] now give a complete filtered differential graded Lie algebra $F^1\mathfrak n$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 By the direct identity $(D+R)^2=[D,R]+[R,R]/2$ and the preceding binary degree and associativity computations, its Maurer–Cartan elements are exactly associative products $\mu+\alpha$ with the specified reduction and with $\alpha$ normalized. Since $\mu(e,a)=a=\mu(a,e)$, normalization is equivalent to $(\mu+\alpha)(e,a)=a=(\mu+\alpha)(a,e)$. Conversely any continuous fixed-unit product with this reduction has such a normalized difference $\alpha$. Hence the claimed object correspondence holds in both directions. In particular at arity two the differential sign is $\pi_1[D,b_\alpha]=-s\delta_\mu\alpha$, while $\pi_1[b_\alpha,b_\alpha]/2=s(\alpha(\alpha(a,b),c)-\alpha(a,\alpha(b,c)))$, so its suspended Maurer–Cartan equation is exactly the expanded associator, with no implicit sign convention. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 On binary Taylor projections, conjugation by $G=T^c(g)$ gives $b_{m'}$ with $m'(a,b)=g(m(g^{-1}a,g^{-1}b))$. If $m$ has unit $e$ and $g(e)=e$, then $m'(e,a)=a=m'(a,e)$; reduction modulo $I$ remains $\mu$. Thus the full subgroup just identified acts on exactly the fixed-unit products in step 7.1, by the stated ordinary transport formula. [step 7.1, step 4.2, step 5.2, algebra]

9.1 The gauge and conjugation proof in [[thm-maurer-cartan-elements-classify-fixed-carrier-codifferential-deformations]] restricts to this normalized subalgebra. In detail its variable unary parameter $\xi(t)$ satisfies $\xi(t)e=0$, and its solution $g'=\xi(t)g$, $g(0)=\operatorname{id}$ has $(g(e)-e)'=\xi(t)(g(e)-e)$ with zero initial value. The same coefficient-order integral induction proves $g(e)=e$. Hence every normalized gauge path has an actual unit-preserving endpoint automorphism. Conversely any allowed unit-preserving $g$ has normalized $\log(g)$ by step 5.2, and $\exp(t\log(g))$ fixes $e$ and gives a normalized gauge path. Therefore normalized gauge equivalence is precisely the entire fixed-unit change-of-variables equivalence, rather than merely the unrestricted codifferential equivalence. [step 6.1, step 5.2, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Finally for $B=k[\![h]\!]$, a continuous coefficient-complete bilinear map is uniquely its sequence of coefficient maps $B_j:A\otimes A\to A$: apply it to constant inputs and expand each output in $A[\![h]\!]$, then use $k[\![h]\!]$-linearity and continuity. Every sequence conversely defines such a map because only finitely many coefficients contribute modulo $h^n$. Reduction fixes the zero coefficient to $\mu$, and normalization is coefficientwise $B_j(e,a)=B_j(a,e)=0$. Thus step 7.1's object bijection and step 9.1's full equivalence correspondence apply to the formal products in the statement, including the initial commutative-algebra case. [step 7.1, step 9.1, construct] ∎
